capstone.title: Field Notes
capstone.subtitle: A small, deployable team notebook with private notes, uploads, search and email.
capstone.goal: Ship a real Django application from an empty project to a public URL with tests, a deployment story and a portfolio write-up.
outcomes: You can model a small domain and defend its boundaries.
You can implement authentication and object-level authorization.
You can build validated forms, uploads and search that stay fast.
You can add one background job and explain why it is asynchronous.
You can deploy with environment settings, static files and migrations.
You can present the result as evidence, not a tutorial.

phases.title: Phase 1 — Domain and data model
phases.brief: Design the smallest useful notebook: users, notebooks, notes, attachments and a soft-delete rule.
tasks: Write a one-page domain model before coding.
Create models with explicit related names and indexes.
Add a `deleted_at` soft-delete field and a manager that hides deleted rows.
Write the first migration and an admin registration.
acceptance: A note always belongs to one notebook and one owner.
Deleted notes are invisible to normal queries.
The admin can inspect notebooks and notes.
The migration applies cleanly on an empty database.

phases.title: Phase 2 — Auth and permissions
phases.brief: Users sign in, see only their notebooks, and get a safe 404 for anything else.
tasks: Add login/logout and a protected dashboard.
Filter every notebook/note queryset by the current user.
Add a test for anonymous access and foreign-object access.
Create a member invitation model with a signed token.
acceptance: Anonymous users are redirected to login.
A user cannot read or edit another user's note.
Invitation tokens expire and are single-purpose.
The permission tests fail if the owner filter is removed.

phases.title: Phase 3 — Forms, uploads and search
phases.brief: Build create/edit forms, validated attachments and a searchable note list.
tasks: Use ModelForm for create/edit with server-controlled owner.
Validate attachment size and image type.
Add search by title/body and paginate the result.
Show a useful empty state and preserve query params.
acceptance: Invalid input re-renders with field errors.
A 3 MB upload is rejected before storage.
Search and pagination preserve the query.
The list page has a constant query count for 20 notes.

phases.title: Phase 4 — One background job and one cache
phases.brief: Send an invitation email asynchronously and cache a dashboard aggregate.
tasks: Move invitation email out of the request path.
Add a retry/error path for the job.
Cache a dashboard count for 60 seconds.
Invalidate the cache when a note or notebook is written.
acceptance: Creating an invitation returns quickly and queues the email.
A failed email is visible in logs and can be retried.
The cached dashboard is invalidated on write.
No per-user data is stored under a shared cache key.

phases.title: Phase 5 — Tests and hardening
phases.brief: Make the project boring to break: tests, checks and a security pass.
tasks: Add tests for the critical permission and upload paths.
Run `manage.py check --deploy` and fix the warnings.
Add CSP or a documented security header strategy.
Add a health endpoint and structured error logging.
acceptance: The critical paths have regression tests.
`check --deploy` passes or has documented exceptions.
Secrets come from environment variables.
A failing health check is visible to the deploy platform.

phases.title: Phase 6 — Deploy and present
phases.brief: Put the app on a public URL and write the portfolio entry.
tasks: Deploy with a managed PostgreSQL database.
Run migrations and collect static files in the release step.
Create a demo account and seed sample data.
Write the README: problem, architecture, tradeoffs, what broke.
acceptance: The app is reachable over HTTPS.
A new user can register, sign in and create a note.
Uploads persist across a redeploy.
The README explains one decision you would change.

deployment: Use environment variables for `SECRET_KEY`, database URL and email credentials.
Run `collectstatic` and serve static files through WhiteNoise or the platform.
Run migrations as a release command, not inside the web process.
Test a rollback or redeploy before calling it done.
portfolio: Repo link with a readable README.
One screenshot of the main workflow.
One hard decision and why you made it.
One failure you found in testing or deployment.
